title: Korean Hangover Soup (Haejang-guk): Types, Recipes and Science
excerpt: What haejang-guk is, the main types of Korean hangover soup, what the science really says about bean sprouts and dried pollack, and two easy recipes to make at home.
metaDescription: Korean hangover soup (haejang-guk) explained: the main types, two easy recipes, and what the science really says about bean sprouts and dried pollack.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Korean hangover soup, called *haejang-guk* (해장국), is one of the most sensible hangover foods in the world, but not because of any magic ingredient. A big bowl of hot, salty broth with protein and vegetables gives you fluid, sodium, and an easy meal at the exact moment your body is short on all three. The popular claims about specific ingredients, like bean sprouts "detoxing" alcohol or dried pollack "protecting the liver," come mostly from lab and animal studies. There is no good evidence from human trials that any one soup speeds up your recovery. It still makes a very good hangover breakfast, and this guide explains the main types, what each one actually offers, and two simple recipes you can make at home.

**The quick picks:** If your stomach is shaky, make **kongnamul-guk** (bean sprout soup). It's light, mild, and takes about 20 minutes. If you can handle something richer, **bugeo-guk** (dried pollack soup) adds protein and an egg. If you're eating out, a Korean restaurant's **seonji haejang-guk** (beef broth with cabbage and ox blood curd) or **ppyeo haejang-guk** (pork spine soup) is the classic order. Whatever you pick, drink water alongside it, go easy on the chili if you have heartburn, and don't add "a little drink to settle things."

## What Is Haejang-guk?

*Haejang-guk* is not one recipe. It's a whole category of Korean soups eaten to recover after a night of drinking. The word breaks down roughly as *haejang* (relieving a hangover, usually traced to older Chinese characters for "releasing" and "hangover") and *guk* (soup). In everyday Korean, *haejang* has become a verb-like idea of its own. People say they're going to "do haejang" the morning after, which simply means eating something to settle their stomach and feel human again.

Korea has a strong after-work drinking culture built around soju, beer, and *makgeolli* (rice wine). Over time, that culture produced a matching food culture for the morning after. You'll find restaurants that serve haejang-guk from early morning, some open around the clock, clustered near office districts and nightlife areas. Different regions are known for their own versions, and many families have a favorite style.

What all the versions share:

- **A hot, savory broth**, usually beef, pork bone, anchovy-kelp, or fish based.
- **Plenty of salt**, from soy sauce, salted shrimp, or fermented soybean paste.
- **Vegetables** such as bean sprouts, radish, napa cabbage, or scallions.
- **A protein**, like beef, pork, fish, egg, or blood curd.
- **Usually rice on the side**, either served separately or dropped right into the bowl.

If you want the bigger picture of why soju in particular can leave you feeling rough, our guide to the [soju hangover](/never-hungover/soju-hangover) covers the drinking side of the story.

## The Main Types of Korean Hangover Soup

Here are the soups you're most likely to meet, from lightest to heaviest.

| Soup | Korean | What's in it | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bean sprout soup | 콩나물국 (kongnamul-guk) | Soybean sprouts, garlic, scallion, clear anchovy or plain broth | Queasy stomach, quick home cooking |
| Bean sprout rice soup | 콩나물국밥 (kongnamul gukbap) | Bean sprout soup with rice in the bowl, often a raw or soft egg | A fuller meal, Jeonju-style |
| Dried pollack soup | 북엇국 (bugeo-guk) | Shredded dried pollack, radish, egg, sesame oil, garlic | Protein without heaviness |
| Ox blood hangover soup | 선지해장국 (seonji haejang-guk) | Beef broth, cabbage leaves, bean sprouts, ox blood curd, soybean paste | The classic restaurant order |
| Napa cabbage soup | 우거지국 (ugeoji-guk) | Outer cabbage leaves in soybean paste broth, often with beef | A milder, earthy option |
| Pork spine soup | 뼈해장국 (ppyeo haejang-guk) | Pork neck bones, potato, cabbage, perilla seeds, chili | Big appetite, late-morning meal |
| Clam soup | 재첩국 (jaecheop-guk) | Tiny freshwater clams in a clear broth with chives | A light seafood option |
| Spicy beef soup | 육개장 (yukgaejang) | Shredded beef, fernbrake, bean sprouts, chili oil | People who want heat |

### Kongnamul-guk (bean sprout soup)

This is the soup most Koreans would make at home. It's nothing more than soybean sprouts simmered in water or a light anchovy-kelp stock, seasoned with garlic, salt or soup soy sauce, and scallions. Some people add a pinch of chili flakes for a little kick. It's cheap, quick, and very gentle on the stomach, which makes it the best first choice if you feel nauseous.

The sprouts are the star. You'll often read that soybean sprouts contain *asparagine* and *aspartic acid*, amino acids that some lab and animal studies have linked to faster breakdown of alcohol by-products. That part is real research, but it is early-stage. Nobody has shown in a proper human trial that a bowl of bean sprout soup clears alcohol or acetaldehyde faster. What the soup clearly does is give you warm fluid, salt, and something easy to eat.

### Kongnamul gukbap (bean sprout rice soup)

The city of Jeonju is famous for this version, where rice goes right into the bowl with the bean sprout soup. It's often served with a soft-cooked or raw egg on the side, plus chopped kimchi and seasoned seaweed. It's more filling than plain kongnamul-guk, so it works well once your stomach has settled a bit.

### Bugeo-guk (dried pollack soup)

*Bugeo* is Alaska pollack that's been dried until it's light and stringy. The shreds are quickly sautéed in sesame oil with garlic, then simmered with water, radish, and a beaten egg that's stirred in at the end. The result is a milky, savory soup that feels restorative without being heavy.

Pollack is a lean, protein-rich fish. Korean food writers often credit it with amino acids, such as methionine, that support the liver. Again, the research behind that claim is mostly animal work using concentrated extracts, not people eating soup. A fair summary is that bugeo-guk is a good source of protein and salt the morning after, and anything beyond that is unproven. A close cousin, *hwangtae haejang-guk*, uses pollack that's been freeze-dried and thawed over a winter, which gives it a fluffier texture.

### Seonji haejang-guk (ox blood hangover soup)

This is the soup many people picture when they hear "haejang-guk." It's a rich beef broth with outer napa cabbage leaves (*ugeoji*), bean sprouts, and soybean paste, with firm cubes of coagulated ox blood (*seonji*). The blood curd has a soft, liver-like texture and a mild taste. If that sounds like a lot, you can usually order it without the seonji.

Blood curd is a good source of iron and protein. That doesn't make it a hangover cure, but it does make the soup a substantial, filling meal.

### Ppyeo haejang-guk (pork spine soup)

Large pork neck bones are simmered for hours with potatoes, cabbage, and a red, slightly spicy broth thickened with ground perilla seeds. It's closely related to *gamjatang*. You eat it slowly, picking the meat off the bones. It's best when your appetite has come back, rather than when you can barely look at food.

### Spicier and seafood options

**Yukgaejang** (spicy shredded beef soup) is a favorite for people who want heat. **Jaecheop-guk**, a clear clam soup from the southern Hadong area, is a light seafood option. Many restaurants also serve **sundae-guk** (blood sausage soup) and **galbitang** (short rib soup) as hangover meals. The same general rule applies to all of them: a hot salty broth with protein and some vegetables.

## What the Science Actually Says

It helps to separate what a hangover is from what soup can realistically do. A hangover is driven by several things at once: dehydration and lost electrolytes, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, low blood sugar in some people, inflammation, and the effects of *acetaldehyde*, a toxic by-product your liver makes while breaking down alcohol. Researchers still argue about how much each of these contributes.

### Where soup genuinely helps

- **Fluid.** Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. A large bowl of broth adds a meaningful amount of fluid in a form that's easy to get down.
- **Sodium and other electrolytes.** A salty broth replaces some of the sodium you lost and helps your body hold on to the fluid you drink. This is the same logic behind drinking an oral rehydration drink.
- **Gentle, easy calories.** Many people feel weak and shaky after drinking. A warm meal with some carbohydrate (rice) and protein helps steady your energy.
- **Something you'll actually eat.** When you feel sick, plain water and dry toast can be hard to face. A savory soup is often more appealing, which matters more than you might think.

### Where the claims run ahead of the evidence

Korean researchers have published a number of studies on traditional hangover ingredients, including soybean sprouts, dried pollack, and various plant extracts. Most of them use cells in a dish or rodents given concentrated extracts. Those studies are worth doing, but they can't tell you what happens when a person eats a bowl of soup the morning after drinking. There is no good evidence that any haejang-guk speeds up how fast your body clears alcohol or acetaldehyde, protects your liver, or shortens a hangover compared with any other decent meal plus water.

That's not a knock on the soups. It just means the benefit is the ordinary, reliable kind: fluid, salt, food, and comfort.

### A note on the "sweat it out" idea

Some people like a fiery bowl because they believe sweating "flushes out" alcohol. Very little alcohol leaves your body through sweat. Almost all of it is broken down by your liver, and that happens at a steady pace you can't speed up by sweating. If spicy food makes you feel better, enjoy it, but sweating also loses fluid, so drink more water to make up for it.

## Recipe: Easy Kongnamul-guk (Bean Sprout Hangover Soup)

This is the version to make when you feel rough and want something done in about 20 minutes. It serves two.

**Ingredients**

- About 10 oz (300 g) soybean sprouts (the ones with yellow heads, not mung bean sprouts), rinsed
- 5 cups water, or anchovy-kelp stock if you have it
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 to 2 scallions, sliced
- 1 tablespoon Korean soup soy sauce (*guk-ganjang*) or regular soy sauce, or salt to taste
- Optional: 1 teaspoon salted shrimp (*saeujeot*) for a deeper savory flavor
- Optional: a pinch of Korean chili flakes (*gochugaru*) or a sliced green chili

**Method**

1. **Make or start the broth.** If you're using a quick anchovy-kelp stock, simmer a handful of dried anchovies (heads and guts removed) and a square of dried kelp in the water for 10 minutes, then strain. Plain water also works fine.
2. **Add the sprouts.** Put the sprouts in the pot, cover with a lid, and bring to a boil. Cook covered for about 5 to 7 minutes. A common Korean tip is to leave the lid on (or off) for the whole cook rather than lifting it halfway, which is said to stop the sprouts tasting raw and "beany."
3. **Season.** Add the garlic and soy sauce or salted shrimp. Taste and adjust the salt. It should taste properly seasoned, not bland.
4. **Finish.** Add the scallions and chili if using, simmer one more minute, and serve hot with a bowl of rice.

**Make it a fuller meal:** crack an egg into the pot for the last two minutes, or put rice straight into the bowl Jeonju-style. Eggs add protein and are easy on the stomach; our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains what they do and don't do.

## Recipe: Bugeo-guk (Dried Pollack Soup)

This takes about 25 minutes and also serves two. Look for bags of shredded dried pollack (*bugeo-chae*) at a Korean grocery store.

**Ingredients**

- 1 large handful (about 1 to 1.5 oz, or 30 to 40 g) shredded dried pollack
- 1 tablespoon toasted sesame oil
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- About 3 oz (a 2-inch piece) Korean radish or daikon, thinly sliced into small squares
- 5 cups water
- 1 egg, beaten
- 1 scallion, sliced
- Salt, soup soy sauce, or a little fish sauce to taste

**Method**

1. **Soften the pollack.** Rinse the pollack shreds briefly under water, squeeze them out, and cut any long pieces into bite-size bits.
2. **Toast it.** Heat the sesame oil in a pot over medium heat and stir-fry the pollack and garlic for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant. This step is what gives the soup its rich, milky look.
3. **Add the radish and water.** Stir in the radish, add the water, and bring to a boil. Simmer for about 10 to 15 minutes until the broth turns cloudy and the radish is tender.
4. **Season.** Add salt or soy sauce to taste.
5. **Add the egg.** Slowly drizzle in the beaten egg while gently stirring, so it forms soft ribbons. Add the scallion, cook one more minute, and serve with rice.

## How to Eat Haejang-guk for the Best Effect

A few small choices make a big difference to how you feel.

- **Drink water too.** Soup helps, but a bowl isn't a full rehydration plan. Keep a glass of water next to you, and sip more through the morning.
- **Go mild if your stomach is upset.** Spicy broths can worsen acid reflux, which is already common after drinking. If you have a burning feeling in your chest, choose a clear soup like kongnamul-guk or bugeo-guk. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers that problem in more detail.
- **Watch the salt if you need to.** Restaurant haejang-guk can be very salty. That's part of why it helps, but if you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease, or have been told to limit sodium, choose a lighter home version and season it gently.
- **Eat slowly.** Small spoonfuls of broth first, then the solid parts as your stomach allows.
- **Add rice for steady energy.** A bit of carbohydrate helps if you feel shaky or weak.
- **Skip the "haejang-sul."** Some people in Korea talk about a morning drink to "chase" the hangover. It only delays the symptoms and adds more alcohol to a body that's still recovering. Our article on [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work) explains why.

## Other Korean Hangover Traditions

Haejang-guk sits within a wider Korean habit of looking after yourself before and after drinking.

- **Hangover drinks and pills.** Korean convenience stores stock a wide range of small bottles and tablets sold for before or after drinking. We review the main ones, and the evidence behind them, in our guide to [Korean and Japanese hangover pills](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills), and the everyday morning-after drinks like honey water and sikhye in our guide to [Korean hangover drinks](/never-hungover/korean-hangover-drinks).
- **Korean pear juice.** Asian pear juice is a popular pre-drinking choice, backed by one small study that's often overstated. Our guide to [Korean pear juice for hangovers](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) looks at what it found.
- **Heotgae tea.** Tea made from the Oriental raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*, called *heotgae-namu* in Korean) is a traditional hangover remedy across East Asia. This tree is also one of the natural sources of **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, the compound many modern hangover supplements are built on. Our [Japanese raisin tree guide](/never-hungover/dhm-japanese-raisin-tree-complete-guide) explains the connection.

If you're comparing haejang-guk with other soups, our roundup of the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) covers pho, ramen, bone broth, and more.

## Where to Find Korean Hangover Soup

- **Korean restaurants.** Most Korean restaurants outside Korea serve at least one of these soups, often listed as haejang-guk, seonji-guk, gamjatang, or yukgaejang. Some open early or stay open late.
- **Korean grocery stores.** Larger Korean and pan-Asian supermarkets usually sell ready-made soups in pouches or in the frozen section, plus the dried pollack, soup soy sauce, and soybean sprouts for making your own.
- **Make a batch ahead.** Kongnamul-guk and bugeo-guk both keep well in the fridge for a few days. If you know you've got a big night coming up, making a pot beforehand means breakfast is ready when you need it.

## When Soup Isn't Enough: Signs to See a Doctor

> **When to get medical help.** A normal hangover is miserable but fades over the day, and soup, water, and rest are the right response. Get help if things don't follow that pattern. **Seek care promptly if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening stomach pain, or you're not peeing or feel faint when you stand up. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if** someone is confused, very hard to wake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has bluish or very pale skin; these are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. If you get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety when you *stop* drinking after a stretch of heavy daily drinking, talk to a doctor; that can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs medical care rather than home remedies.

## A Practical Morning-After Routine

Putting it all together, here's a simple plan that uses haejang-guk sensibly:

1. **Water first.** A glass or two as soon as you're up.
2. **Soup as breakfast.** A bowl of kongnamul-guk or bugeo-guk with rice, eaten slowly.
3. **More fluids through the morning.** Water, or an electrolyte drink if you were sweating or vomiting.
4. **A pain reliever only if you need it, and carefully.** Take it with food and follow the label. If you're unsure which one suits you after drinking, ask a pharmacist.
5. **Rest.** Sleep after drinking is usually poor quality, so a nap or an easy day helps more than any single food.

The bigger wins come before the next night out. Eating a proper meal before drinking, pacing yourself, and alternating drinks with water have far better support than any morning-after remedy. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through those habits.

## Where DHM Fits In

Haejang-guk helps the morning after. Some people also want something to take on the night itself. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound found in the Oriental raisin tree, the same tree behind traditional Korean heotgae tea. Lab and animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and may support the liver, and there's a small amount of human data, but the evidence is still early. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it's no substitute for drinking less and eating well.

If you'd like to try it, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, budget-friendly single-ingredient option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- *Haejang-guk* is a family of Korean hangover soups, not a single dish. The most common are bean sprout soup, dried pollack soup, and beef broth with cabbage and ox blood curd.
- They help for ordinary reasons: fluid, salt, protein, easy calories, and a warm meal you'll actually want to eat.
- Claims that particular ingredients detox alcohol or protect your liver come mostly from lab and animal studies. There is no good evidence that any one soup shortens a hangover.
- Choose a mild, clear soup if your stomach is upset or you have heartburn, and go easy on the salt if you need to limit sodium.
- Drink water alongside your soup, skip the morning drink, and get medical help if you can't keep fluids down or see signs of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is Korean hangover soup called?**

It's called *haejang-guk* (해장국), which roughly means "soup to relieve a hangover." It's a category of soups rather than one recipe. The most common types are kongnamul-guk (bean sprout soup), bugeo-guk (dried pollack soup), and seonji haejang-guk (beef broth with napa cabbage and ox blood curd).

**Does Korean hangover soup actually work?**

It helps, but for everyday reasons. A hot, salty broth gives you fluid and sodium, and the protein, vegetables, and rice give you an easy meal when your body needs one. Claims that bean sprouts or dried pollack speed up alcohol breakdown come mostly from lab and animal studies. There is no good evidence that any particular soup shortens a hangover more than a decent meal and plenty of water.

**What is the best Korean soup for a hangover?**

If your stomach is upset, kongnamul-guk (bean sprout soup) is the best place to start because it's light, mild, and quick to make. Bugeo-guk (dried pollack soup) adds more protein without being heavy. If you're hungry and eating out, seonji haejang-guk or ppyeo haejang-guk (pork spine soup) are the classic restaurant choices.

**Why do Koreans eat bean sprout soup for a hangover?**

Bean sprout soup is cheap, quick, and gentle on the stomach, and it has been a home hangover remedy in Korea for generations. Soybean sprouts contain amino acids such as asparagine, which some lab and animal studies have linked to faster processing of alcohol by-products. Those findings haven't been confirmed in human trials, so the main proven benefits are fluid, salt, and an easy meal.

**Is spicy soup good for a hangover?**

It can be, if your stomach handles it. Some people find a spicy broth helps them feel more awake. But spicy food can worsen heartburn and acid reflux, which are common after drinking, and sweating from chili means losing a bit more fluid. Very little alcohol leaves the body through sweat, so you can't "sweat it out." If you have a burning stomach, choose a mild, clear soup instead.

**What is the ox blood in Korean hangover soup?**

It's called *seonji*: ox blood that has been coagulated into firm, jelly-like cubes. It has a soft texture and a mild, slightly iron-rich taste, and it adds protein and iron to the soup. If you'd rather not eat it, most restaurants will serve the soup without it.

**Can I make Korean hangover soup ahead of time?**

Yes. Bean sprout soup and dried pollack soup both keep in the fridge for a few days in a covered container. Making a pot before a big night means you have an easy, hydrating breakfast ready the next morning. Reheat it until it's steaming hot before eating.

**Is Korean hangover soup too salty?**

Restaurant versions can be very salty. The salt is part of why the soup helps after drinking, since it replaces sodium and helps you hold on to fluid. But if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or kidney disease, or have been told to limit sodium, choose a home-made version, season it lightly, and drink water with it.
